## Key Terms

**Audit query library.** A documented set of saved queries that perform an organization's recurring audit tests, each stating its objective, population, reconciliation, expected result, and the disposition of its exceptions, so that the tests can be rerun every period.

**Concentration of approval.** A condition in which one person approves most or all of the documents in a process, so that the approval control depends on that person alone. It is a risk rather than an exception in any one document, and it can indicate a weakness in the design of the control.

**Cutoff.** The recording of a transaction in the accounting period in which it occurred. A cutoff test compares the posting date of each transaction's ledger rows with the date of the event behind it, such as the delivery of the goods a sales invoice bills or the work a payroll pays, and flags the transactions recorded in a different period.

**Existence and completeness tests.** Tests that trace in opposite directions between the ledger and its documents. An existence test starts from the ledger and asks whether each posting has a document record; a completeness test starts from the documents and asks whether each was posted. The second is an audit assertion about the ledger, not the data quality dimension of Chapter 2, which asks whether the expected records and values are present in a dataset.

**Full-population testing.** An audit approach that applies a test to every item of a population rather than to a sample, so that it finds the actual exceptions instead of estimating an error rate.

**Goods received not invoiced.** The liability for goods or services received from suppliers before their invoices have been recorded. Its balance should agree with the value of the receipts not yet invoiced.

**Price tolerance.** The difference between an invoice price and an order price that a match accepts without investigation, set in advance from the purchasing policy. Differences above it are exceptions.

**Self-join.** A join of a table to itself, under two aliases, used to compare each row with other rows of the same table, such as payments to the same supplier for the same amount on different dates. A condition such as `b.ID > a.ID` keeps each pair once.

**Substantive analytical procedure.** An analytical procedure that an auditor uses as evidence about whether an amount is misstated, by comparing the recorded amount with an expectation developed from plausible relationships and investigating differences above a threshold set in advance. In SQL, the expectation can be calculated for every record of a population, as when the hours of each earnings line times the employee's rate of pay predict the amount paid.

**Three-way match.** A comparison of the purchase order, the goods receipt, and the supplier invoice for the same purchase, testing that the company is billed only for what it ordered and received, at the price it approved.

**UNION ALL.** An operator that stacks the results of two or more queries with the same number of columns into one result, matching the columns by position and keeping every row. UNION, without ALL, also removes duplicate rows.

**Unrecorded liability.** An obligation that exists at the balance sheet date but is missing from the ledger, such as goods received but never recorded, or wages earned but not yet paid. A reconciliation cannot find it, because it is missing from both records; the auditor looks for it in the invoices and payments after the year-end and in the dates of the events behind them.
